data.title: Middle East Eye: Saudi Arabia turns to UAE 'white horse' as it gears up to battle Yemen's Houthis
data.author: Mera Aladam
data.summary:
Saudi Arabia turns to UAE 'white horse' as it gears up to battle Yemen's Houthis
Saudi Arabia appears to be mending fences with the UAE in an effort to push back a Houthi military offensive in Yemen that threatens the kingdom’s Red Sea oil export corridor and has seen drones strike Riyadh.
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman hosted the UAE’s vice president, Mansour Bin Zayed, in Riyadh on Tuesday, marking the kingdom's most prominent effort yet to reconcile with the UAE after clashing over Sudan, Yemen, and Somaliland.
“The Houthis are bringing Saudi Arabia and the UAE closer together,” Anna Jacobs, a non-resident fellow at the Arab Gulf States Institute, told Middle East Eye.
The two neighbours have been discussing how to collaborate on Yemen for months, western and Arab officials tell MEE, but the talks have been moving slowly.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Qatar's prime minister calls Netanyahu 'war criminal', says Doha will continue diplomacy efforts in region
data.author: Mera Aladam
data.summary:
Qatar's prime minister calls Netanyahu 'war criminal', says Doha will continue diplomacy efforts in region
Qatar's prime minister accused his Israeli counterpart, Benjamin Netanyahu, of being a "war criminal", and stressed that Doha would continue its mediation efforts despite escalating tensions in the region.
During an interview with Piers Morgan, Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani - who is also Qatar's foreign minister - was asked whether he considered Netanyahu a war criminal.
He responded by saying: "Of course. What’s been committed in Gaza is war crimes, and whoever is responsible for this is a war criminal."
"Hospitals have been targeted, schools have been targeted. Whatever the justifications and the arguments, nothing is justifying this," he added.
The Qatari prime minister also brought up Israel's attack on Qatar in early September of last year, when it targeted Hamas officials while Doha was engaged in mediation efforts.
"We were attacked by Israel while we were mediating," he said. "Netanyahu has crossed the line like he has crossed other lines before that."
Despite escalating regional tensions, he indicated Qatar's readiness in ongoing diplomacy and mediation efforts.
"We are trying to do our best to give the best advice to the US government on how to reach a solution, as well as to the Iranians," he said.

Israel's opposition leader accuses Netanyahu of fearmongering ahead of elections
Israeli opposition leader Yair Lapid accused Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of stoking security fears by claiming that enemies might attack ahead of the 27 October elections.
Lapid reportedly requested an urgent security briefing after Netanyahu on Tuesday said that there were "indications" that Israel’s enemies could try to attack the country before elections began.
The prime minister's claims came during a visit to Tel Nof Airbase in central Israel.
"Netanyahu ignored every warning before October 7 and now, 28 days before the election, he’s suddenly busy fearmongering," Lapid said.
After the meeting late on Tuesday, Lapid asserted that "there is no reason to panic the public", adding that Israeli military bases "are not the setting for election videos".
"I of course will not violate the confidentiality of the security briefing but it must be said - security threats must be handled professionally and responsibly," Lapid said.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Shobeiri Zanjani: The quiet ayatollah who bridged Iran’s political divide
data.author: MEE correspondent
data.summary:
Shobeiri Zanjani: The quiet ayatollah who bridged Iran’s political divide
Submitted by
MEE correspondent
on
Mon, 09/28/2026 - 12:38
Grand Ayatollah Mousa Shobeiri Zanjani passed away on 20 September at the age of 98
Grand Ayatollah Mousa Shobeiri Zanjani was a highly respected and influential religious figure across Iran's political spectrum (X)
Off
When Grand Ayatollah Mousa Shobeiri Zanjani died at 98 on 20 September, he left behind a rare position in Iran’s religious establishment: a cleric who kept his distance from political power, yet whose influence reached across the Islamic Republic’s deepest political divides.
His students included former reformist President Mohammad Khatami and, according to a source in the Qom Seminary, Mojtaba Khamenei, the current supreme leader. For decades, politicians and clerics on opposing sides of Iran’s political spectrum turned to Shobeiri because his authority rested outside politics.
That independence made him an important figure at moments when Iran’s political and religious establishments collided.
Shobeiri was one of seven senior clerics identified by the Society of Seminary Scholars of Qom in the 1990s as qualified to be followed as a grand ayatollah and serve as a marja, or religious authority.
The ayatollah belonged to a strand of the Iranian clergy that believed clerics should not directly enter politics.
They are often described as “traditional” clerics, a group that includes Ayatollah Vahid Khorasani, another highly respected figure in the seminary establishment. Both men have largely stayed outside of the Islamic Republic's factional politics.
Traditional clerics tend to see their role primarily as preserving the independence of the seminaries from the state, maintaining the institution of marjaʿiyyah – the system of senior religious authorities whom believers may follow for guidance on matters of Islamic law – and addressing religious and social affairs rather than directly participating in political power.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Vietnam taught America the limits of its power. Hormuz is teaching it again
data.author: Sami Al-Arian
data.summary:
Vietnam taught America the limits of its power. Hormuz is teaching it again
Submitted by
Sami Al-Arian
on
Tue, 09/29/2026 - 17:43
Washington believed the 1991 Gulf War had overcome the 'Vietnam Syndrome'. Seven months of bombing and blockade against Iran have brought it back
Vessels sit in the Strait of Hormuz near Bandar Abbas, Iran, on 28 September 2026, a week after commercial crossings of the strait fell to two in a single day (Amirhosein Khorgooi/ISNA/WANA via Reuters)
On
On 22 September, only two commercial vessels crossed the Strait of Hormuz. A narrow choke point that normally handles a fifth of the world's daily oil supply, as well as a fifth of globally traded liquefied natural gas, sits almost silent under the watch of multibillion-dollar American warships that cannot convince commercial insurers to risk even a handful of tankers.
Washington can still destroy almost anything it targets across the Middle East, but whether that destruction can buy the political outcome it wants is a vastly different question.
Seven months into the war against Iran that began on 28 February 2026, Washington has cycled through three strategies of coercion: massive aerial bombardment, economic strangulation through a naval blockade and direct tit-for-tat escalation. None restored normal passage through the strait.
The US military can dominate the skies, sink ships and eliminate political and military leaders, yet it remains unable to compel Tehran to accept its terms.
Vietnam, the Gulf War of 1991 and the current war in the Gulf belong to different eras and involve radically different adversaries that cannot be mechanically equated, yet each tells us something important about the limits and reach of American power.
The "Vietnam Syndrome" was more than a domestic aversion to casualties. It was a crisis of confidence in the efficacy, morality and political utility of American military power.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Israeli attacks caused 70 percent of recorded Gaza deaths in 2025
data.author: Elis Gjevori
data.summary:
Israeli attacks caused 70 percent of recorded Gaza deaths in 2025
Israeli forces’ attacks caused 70.1 percent of the 24,650 deaths the Palestinian health ministry in Gaza registered last year, according to its first official mortality report since 2022.
The under-five mortality rate more than doubled, reaching 33.4 deaths per 1,000 live births in 2025 compared with 13.6 in 2022. Excluding war deaths, the ministry put the rate at 15.8.
Heart disease accounted for 7.7 percent of recorded deaths, making it the second-largest cause. Males represented 73.4 percent of those who died and females 26.6 percent.
Gaza City accounted for the largest share of deaths at 37.3 percent. The North Gaza governorate followed with 20.2 percent, ahead of Khan Younis at 19.5 percent, the Middle Area at 12.3 percent and Rafah at 10.7 percent.

Israeli drone hits Gaza shelter as attacks wound six Palestinians despite ceasefire
Two children are among six Palestinians wounded in fresh Israeli attacks in Gaza despite the ceasefire, according to local sources cited by the official Wafa news agency.
A drone targeted a shelter housing displaced people in southern Gaza, injuring four people, including the children. One of the wounded was reportedly in a serious condition.
Israeli soldiers also seriously wounded two Palestinians southeast of Deir el-Balah in central Gaza.
